job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a software developer at a logistics company in Aarhus, working on the system that plans delivery routes for supermarket trucks. I studied computer science at Aarhus University, and my final project was a route planner for a local food bank. A normal day is code, a team lunch, and a bike ride home to the flat I share with my sister Salma. Evenings are family dinners, and Fridays I go to the mosque with my mother. I use an AI assistant for some code, but I check it carefully and I wouldn't paste company data into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reasonable, and it matches what I see. I'd tell friends use the tools where they help, but don't believe the big stories. At work we'd carry on as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fine. Routes and delivery are physical things in the real world, and software has to deal with strikes, weather and broken trucks. I'd still worry about housing, because Aarhus rents are high and I'd like my own place before I marry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and save for a flat. I'd get better at the tools slowly, and I'd keep going to the mosque and family events. I'd say yes to the senior role if they offered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, grateful. I'm lucky to have this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like your own place before you marry. What's the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents say a daughter should have a safe home, and they'd help with part of a deposit. I'd like to pay most myself, so I'm saving 7,000 a month. In four years I could buy a small flat near the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check the AI assistant carefully. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I read every line and run the tests twice. Once it invented a function that doesn't exist, and I only noticed because my colleague Lars asked what it did. Since then I trust it like a bright trainee, who needs watching.

say: The tools help, but **don't believe** the big stories about them.
At work we'd carry on as usual, with the same backlog and deadlines.
think: Routes involve strikes, weather and broken trucks, so my job feels **secure**.
I worry about **housing**, because Aarhus rents are high.
do: Save **7,000 a month** toward a small flat near the harbour.
Get better at the tools **slowly** and accept a senior role if offered.
feel: I feel **calm and grateful** for this job.
S0.quote: I trust it like a bright trainee, who needs watching.
fieldNote: She is secure and **grateful**, with housing as the only pressure.
She treats AI like a trainee and keeps company data out of it.
Her family backs her but she prefers to pay herself.

steps.text: Save 7,000 kroner a month for a flat near the harbour
Keep checking every AI answer line by line before I use it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but we've seen big changes before. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and keep their values. At work I'd say let's agree rules for how we use AI with customer data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes more than I'd like. The code I write now could be done by a good AI in a few minutes. The part that stays is knowing what the supermarkets need and how to keep promises. I'd want to be a person they trust, not a coder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to take part in customer meetings and learn more about how the supermarkets work. I'd use AI more in my own tasks, since being seen as slow would hurt. And I'd talk with my family about whether to marry earlier, because a stable family makes the rest easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I trust that we'll manage, and I also feel a tightness in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk about marrying earlier. Why would that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a household has two people watching out for each other. My parents have been through a move from another country and lost jobs, and they say it's the marriage that holds. I'm not in a hurry, but I'd want to talk to a man who shares my values and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would those customer meetings give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd give me a bit of trust, which is what the AI can't make. A supermarket manager phones when a truck is late, and wants a person who says I'll fix it. I'd like to be that voice, even if the code is written by something else.

say: It's a big change, but we've seen big changes before, so **keep your values**.
At work I'd set rules for AI and customer data.
think: My job changes more than I'd like, since AI could write my **code** in minutes.
What stays is knowing what supermarkets need and **keeping promises**.
do: Join **customer meetings** and learn how the supermarkets work.
Use AI more in my own tasks and talk to family about **marrying earlier**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, trusting we'll manage but with a tight chest.
S1.quote: A supermarket manager phones when a truck is late, and wants a person who says I'll fix it.
fieldNote: She turns toward **trust and people work**, the part software lacks.
Her faith and family shape how she plans her life.
She admits a physical sign of worry, a tight chest.

steps.text: Ask my manager to put me in weekly meetings with supermarket customers
Use the AI assistant for my routine coding tasks
Talk with my parents about bringing a marriage forward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is hard, but we have our faith and each other. I'd tell friends to save and to stay close to family. At work I'd ask the management for honesty about what they plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. If AI can do most thinking work in two years, a logistics software team could be cut by a lot. I'd be one of the less experienced, and I've only been here a year. I'd feel it would be sensible to prepare for a long period without a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put almost everything into savings and delay the flat. I'd ask my parents if I can move back into the family home for a while to save rent. And I'd talk to my uncle, who owns a small delivery firm, about working with him if things got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying more, and checking the news more than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your uncle owns a delivery firm. What would you do there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help with routes, billing, and customer messages, and I'd bring the tools I know. It's not glamorous, but it's family and it's real. My uncle has said before that there's always a seat for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving back home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud and not proud. My mother would be happy to have me and my father would say it's what a family is for. I'd feel I stepped back, but I'd also feel safe, and I'd try to accept the safe part.

say: Two years is hard, but we have our **faith and each other**.
I'd ask management to be honest about what they plan.
think: A logistics software team could be cut by a lot, and I'm among the **least experienced**.
I should prepare for a long time without a **salary**.
do: Put almost everything into **savings** and delay the flat.
Plan to move back to my **parents'** home, with my uncle's delivery firm as a fallback.
feel: I feel **anxious**, praying more and checking the news too much.
S2.quote: My uncle has said before that there's always a seat for me.
fieldNote: Family is her **safety net**, with a real fallback job at her uncle's firm.
She feels both pride and shame about moving home.
Her junior status makes her expect to be cut early.

steps.text: Put 80 percent of my pay into savings and delay buying a flat
Ask my parents if I can move back home to save rent
Talk to my uncle about helping with routes and billing at his delivery firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a time to get organised. I'd tell friends and the mosque youth group that skills and community will matter. At work I'd say let's plan how juniors learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect the middle years to be hard but manageable. By 2031 some of what I do is automated, but companies still need people they trust to run it. I'd want to be that person, probably in a team lead or customer role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study some business and logistics on the side, aiming for an operations role. I'd marry in about three years, with someone who shares my values. I'd keep saving for the flat. I'd use AI a bit more every year as it proves reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but steady. I think the five years let me build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mosque youth group. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn a real skill, be kind and don't compare yourself to people online. Some of the boys feel they're already too late. I'd tell them that a good character and a trade are worth more than any fashionable course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why business and logistics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know how the trucks move. If I understand costs and contracts too, I could run a depot or manage a customer account. Those roles still need a person who answers the phone and signs the form.

say: Five years is a time to get **organised**, and skills and community will matter.
I'd tell the mosque youth group to build a real skill.
think: The middle years are hard but manageable, and companies still need **trusted people** to run the systems.
I'd aim for a team lead or customer role.
do: Study **business and logistics** on the side for an operations role.
Marry in about three years and keep saving for the **flat**.
feel: I feel **uneasy but steady**, because five years let me build.
S3.quote: A good character and a trade are worth more than any fashionable course.
fieldNote: Time lets her **widen her skills** into operations, which machines reach later.
She sees mentoring younger people as part of her role.
Marriage plans fit a longer timeline.

steps.text: Study logistics and business part time at the university
Aim for a depot manager or customer account role
Plan a wedding in about three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous. I'd tell everyone to build skills and stay close to family. At work I'd say let's slow down and train people properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calmer. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married with a child and in a more senior job. The big changes would be there, but I'd have grown up with them. I'd worry about my parents' health care, and how it's paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and save, buy a flat in about four years, and have a child by around 28. I'd go to the mosque and give to charity. I'd try to become a manager and learn how to lead people in a world of machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I can imagine my life, and it looks good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your parents' health care. What is the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father has a bad back from years of driving a taxi, and my mother is diabetic. Denmark's system is good, but waiting times grow. If AI helps with diagnosis, I'd welcome it, and if it only saves money for the state, I'd want it to be shared fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leading people in a world of machines look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means being fair, listening, and knowing when to ask a person instead of a system. I want to be a manager who remembers that the person on the phone has a family. That part I learned from my mother, who ran a small shop.

say: Ten years is generous, so build skills and **stay close to family**.
At work I'd slow down and train people properly.
think: By 32 I'd be married with a **child** and in a more senior job.
I'd worry about my parents' **health care** and how it's paid.
do: Buy a **flat** in about four years and have a child by about 28.
Become a **manager** and give to charity.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, because I can imagine my life.
S4.quote: I want to be a manager who remembers that the person on the phone has a family.
fieldNote: Ten years softens her fear, but **parents' health care** keeps her uneasy.
Her leadership model comes from her mother's shop.
Her plans combine family, faith and a managerial path.

steps.text: Buy a flat in about four years
Apply for a team lead role within three years
Give a fixed share of my pay to charity each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because it leaves no time for a young person to build savings or a family. What would help is honesty from employers, retraining that comes with pay, and protection for people with health problems or care duties.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume young people in tech are all secular and individualist. I'm not. I think community and faith are what get you through times like this.

headlineQuote: I think community and faith are what get you through times like this.
portrait: Aisha is a **22-year-old** developer at a logistics firm in Aarhus, top of her class.
She is traditional, family and faith-centred, and uses AI **now and then**, with care.
Her **uncle's delivery firm** and her parents' home give her real fallbacks.
She is calm in a plateau, and **anxious** only when two years threaten her savings.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, since it leaves no time to build savings or a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest employers**, paid retraining and protection for people with health or care duties.
